1. Introduction

This Privacy Policy explains how information is collected, used, and protected when you visit franziska-zimmer.com.
The website is operated for academic and informational purposes.

By using this website, you agree to the practices described in this policy.

2. Information Collected Through the Contact Form

When you contact the website through the contact form, the following information may be collected:

  • Name
  • Email address
  • Message content

This information is provided voluntarily by users and is used only for the purpose of responding to inquiries or communication related to academic or professional matters.

Your information will not be sold, shared, or distributed to third parties unless required by law.

3. Automatically Collected Information

When you visit this website, certain technical information may be automatically collected through standard web server logs. This may include:

  • IP address
  • Browser type
  • Device type
  • Operating system
  • Date and time of access
  • Referring pages
  • Pages visited on this site

These logs are used solely for the purpose of:

  • maintaining website security
  • diagnosing technical issues
  • analyzing website usage and improving the site

This information does not directly identify individual visitors.

4. Cookies and Analytics

This website may use cookies or similar technologies to improve the user experience and analyze website traffic.

Cookies are small text files stored on your device. They help the website understand how visitors interact with the site.

You can disable cookies through your browser settings if you prefer not to allow them.

If analytics tools (such as Google Analytics) are used, they may collect anonymized usage information to help understand visitor behavior and improve website content.

5. Data Security

Reasonable technical and organizational measures are taken to protect personal information from unauthorized access, misuse, or disclosure.

However, please note that no internet transmission or electronic storage system can be guaranteed to be completely secure.

6. External Links

This website may contain links to external websites such as:

  • Google Scholar
  • ResearchGate
  • ACM Digital Library

These external sites have their own privacy policies. This website is not responsible for the content or privacy practices of those websites.

7. Data Retention

Information submitted through the contact form may be retained only as long as necessary to respond to inquiries or maintain professional communication.

Server log data may be retained for security and administrative purposes.

8. Changes to This Privacy Policy

This Privacy Policy may be updated periodically.

9. Contact

If you have questions regarding this Privacy Policy or the handling of personal data, you may contact:

I study user behavior in digital systems using large-scale data.

I am Franziska Zimmer, a researcher in information science and human-computer interaction, focusing on the analysis of user behavior through log data, surveys, and computational methods. My work examines how users interact with digital systems, how behavioral patterns can be identified at scale, and how these patterns differ across users and environments.

My current research focuses on behavioral data analysis in digital systems, including work on behavioral biometrics and user interaction patterns. I analyze large-scale datasets to understand how users behave within complex systems and how interaction data can be used to distinguish and characterize user behavior.

Previously, I conducted research on user behavior in online platforms, including social media and misinformation. Using a combination of content analysis, surveys, and behavioral data, I studied how users interact with information and how behavior differs across platforms and user groups. Through my research and teaching, I aim to better understand user behavior in real-world digital environments and contribute to data-driven insights about how people interact with modern systems.

About

About me

I am a researcher in user behavior and human-computer interaction, specializing in large-scale data analysis, log data, and survey-based methods to understand how users interact with digital systems.

Researcher in data-driven information science & digital systems

My work focuses on analyzing behavioral patterns using interaction data, surveys, and computational methods. I study how user behavior can be measured and analyzed at scale, and how behavioral signals can be used to identify patterns across users and understand differences in how people interact with digital systems.

My research spans three main areas:

  • Large-scale behavioral data analysis, including log data, spatiotemporal data, and pattern analysis
  • Quantitative and mixed-methods user research, including surveys, interviews, and behavioral measurement
  • Analysis of online behavior and user-generated content, including forums, social media, and communication patterns

To support this work, I apply a range of quantitative and computational approaches, including log data analysis, statistical modeling, machine learning for classification and pattern detection, survey design and analysis, and large-scale content analysis.

My work includes analyzing datasets ranging from hundreds of users to tens of millions of records to uncover behavioral patterns in real-world systems, with the goal of generating insights that help better understand user behavior in digital environments.

Currently, I am a Project Assistant Professor at the Graduate School of Information Science and Technology at The University of Tokyo, where I am affiliated with the Social ICT Research Center and Yamaguchi Laboratory. My research focuses on behavioral biometrics and user behavior analysis in large-scale digital systems.

Previously, I conducted research and teaching at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Germany, where I studied user behavior on social media, misinformation, and information interaction in online environments.

Experience

The University of Tokyo, Graduate School of Information Science and Technology​

2024 – Present Assistant Professor 2023 – 2024 Project Researcher

I work as an Assistant Professor at the Rie Yamaguchi Lab, where I conduct research on user behavior in large-scale digital systems. My work focuses on analyzing interaction data, behavioral patterns, and spatiotemporal data to understand how users engage with complex systems. My research includes behavioral log analysis and machine learning approaches to identify patterns in user interaction data, particularly in the context of behavior-based authentication. I work with datasets ranging from hundreds of users to millions of records, applying statistical and computational methods to uncover meaningful behavioral signals.

Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf, Department of Information Science

2018 – 2023 Research Associate & Lecturing 2020 – 2023 PhD in Information Science

I conducted research on user behavior in online environments, with a focus on social media, misinformation, and how users interact with information across digital platforms. This work formed the basis of my PhD research under the supervision of Prof. Wolfgang G. Stock. My research involved analyzing large-scale user-generated content (e.g., forums, livestreams) and combining content analysis with quantitative methods to study communication patterns and user behavior. I worked with multiple data sources, including surveys, behavioral data, and platform content, to understand how users engage with information in real-world environments. This included studies across different platforms (e.g., livestreaming, online forums) and diverse user groups, including vulnerable populations, to examine differences in behavior and information interaction. In addition to research, I designed and taught courses and supervised student research projects in information science and user behavior.

Trivago N.V., Düsseldorf, Search Technology – Advertiser Quality Management

2014 – 2015 Working Student

Analyzed search and advertiser data to identify quality issues and support improvements in platform results and user-facing data accuracy.​

Franziska Zimmer

フランジスカ・ジマー

インタビュー記事・メディア掲載 インタビュー記事 WIRED

TikTokで“24時間365日ライブ配信”をする人たちと夢中になる視聴者。その双方の事情とは

記事を読む → メディア紹介 Forbes

ライブ配信者と「退屈さ」がもたらす影響とは

記事を読む → インタビュー記事 Compliance Corylated

Twitchの予測市場のゲーム化は若者にリスクをもたらす

記事を読む →

大規模データを活用し、デジタル環境におけるユーザー行動を研究しています

情報科学およびヒューマン・コンピュータ・インタラクションを専門とする研究者、フランジスカ・ジマーと申します。ログデータ、アンケート、計算手法を組み合わせることで、ユーザー行動の分析に取り組んでいます。デジタルシステムにおいてユーザーがどのように行動し、そのパターンがどのように大規模に把握できるのか、またユーザーや環境によってどのように異なるのかを明らかにすることを研究テーマとしています。

現在は、デジタルシステムにおける行動データ分析に焦点を当て、行動バイオメトリクスやユーザーのインタラクションパターンに関する研究を進めています。大規模データセットを用いて、複雑なシステム内でのユーザーの行動を理解し、インタラクションデータから個々の行動特性を識別・特徴付けることを目指しています。

これまでには、ソーシャルメディアや誤情報を含むオンラインプラットフォームにおけるユーザー行動について研究を行ってきました。コンテンツ分析、アンケート、行動データを組み合わせることで、ユーザーが情報とどのように関わり、プラットフォームやユーザー層によって行動がどのように異なるのかを分析してきました。研究と教育を通じて、実社会のデジタル環境におけるユーザー行動の理解を深め、人とシステムの関係性に関するデータ駆動型の知見の提供を目指しています。

title: プロフィール
description: プロフィール Franziska Zimmer（フランジスカ・ジマー） ユーザー行動とヒューマン・コンピュータ・インタラクション（HCI）を専門とする情報科学者です。 大規模データ分析やログデータ、アンケート調査などの手法を用いて、ユーザーがデジタルシステムとどのように関わっているのかを明らかにする研究に取り
html:
プロフィール

Franziska Zimmer（フランジスカ・ジマー）

ユーザー行動とヒューマン・コンピュータ・インタラクション（HCI）を専門とする情報科学者です。
大規模データ分析やログデータ、アンケート調査などの手法を用いて、ユーザーがデジタルシステムとどのように関わっているのかを明らかにする研究に取り組んでいます。

データ駆動型情報科学・デジタルシステムの研究

私の研究は、インタラクションデータやアンケート、計算的手法を組み合わせてユーザーの行動パターンを分析することに重点を置いています。

ユーザー行動をどのように測定し、大規模に分析できるのか、そしてそこからどのような特徴や違いが見えてくるのかを探っています。

研究分野は主に次の3つです：

・ログデータや時空間データを用いた大規模な行動分析

・アンケートやインタビューを含む定量・混合手法によるユーザー研究

・ソーシャルメディアやフォーラムなどにおけるオンライン行動・ユーザー生成コンテンツの分析

これらの研究では、ログ分析、統計モデリング、機械学習（分類・パターン検出）、アンケート設計・分析など、さまざまな手法を活用しています。

また、数百人規模から数千万件規模までのデータを対象に分析を行い、現実のデジタル環境におけるユーザー行動の理解を深めることを目指しています。

現在は、東京大学大学院情報理工学系研究科にて特任助教として研究に従事し、ソーシャルICT研究センターおよび山口研究室に所属しています。

主に、大規模デジタルシステムにおけるユーザー行動分析や行動バイオメトリクスに関する研究を行っています。

これまでには、ドイツのハインリヒ・ハイネ大学デュッセルドルフにて研究・教育に携わり、ソーシャルメディアや誤情報、オンライン環境における情報との関わり方についての研究を行ってきました。

経歴

東京大学 大学院情報理工学系研究科

2024年 – 現在
特任助教
2023年 – 2024年
特任研究員

山口利恵研究室において助教として勤務し、大規模デジタルシステムにおけるユーザー行動の研究に従事しています。主にインタラクションデータ、行動パターン、時空間データの分析を通じて、ユーザーが複雑なシステムとどのように関わるのかを解明することを目的としています。
行動ログ解析や機械学習手法を用いて、ユーザーインタラクションデータに潜むパターンを特定し、特に行動ベース認証の文脈において研究を進めています。数百人規模から数百万レコード規模のデータセットを扱い、統計的および計算的手法を活用して有意義な行動シグナルの抽出を行っています。

ハインリヒ・ハイネ大学デュッセルドルフ 情報科学学科

2018年 – 2023年
研究員・講師
2020年 – 2023年
情報科学 博士（PhD）

オンライン環境におけるユーザー行動の研究に従事し、特にソーシャルメディア、誤情報、そしてユーザーがデジタルプラットフォーム上で情報とどのように関わるかに焦点を当てました。本研究は、Wolfgang G. Stock教授の指導のもとで博士研究として発展しました。
ユーザー生成コンテンツ（フォーラムやライブ配信など）を対象に、大規模データ分析を実施し、コンテンツ分析と定量的手法を組み合わせることで、コミュニケーションパターンおよびユーザー行動を明らかにしました。アンケート、行動データ、プラットフォームデータなど複数のデータソースを活用し、実環境における情報利用行動を分析しました。
また、ライブ配信やオンラインフォーラムなど複数のプラットフォームにおいて、異なるユーザー層（脆弱な立場のユーザーを含む）間の行動差異についても研究を行いました。
教育面では、講義の設計・実施および学生の研究指導にも携わりました。

Trivago N.V.（デュッセルドルフ）検索技術部門

2014年 – 2015年
ワーキングスチューデント

検索データおよび広告主データを分析し、品質上の課題を特定するとともに、検索結果の改善およびユーザー向けデータの精度向上に貢献しました。

title: Prediction Markets and the Dynamics of Collective Information
description: 1. Introduction: The Rise of Prediction Markets Prediction markets have become an increasingly visible component of digital information ecosystems. Origina
html:
1. Introduction: The Rise of Prediction Markets

Prediction markets have become an increasingly visible component of digital information ecosystems. Originally developed as tools for forecasting events such as elections or economic indicators, prediction markets now appear in a wide range of online environments. These markets allow participants to trade contracts representing possible future outcomes, with prices reflecting the collective probability assigned to those outcomes.

The basic idea behind prediction markets is relatively simple: when individuals with diverse information participate in a market, their combined decisions may produce more accurate forecasts than those made by a single expert or centralized authority. Market prices continuously adjust as participants respond to new information, creating a dynamic representation of collective expectations.

In recent years, the rapid expansion of digital platforms has transformed how prediction markets operate. Online systems allow thousands of participants to interact in real time, generating large volumes of data that reflect changing beliefs about uncertain events. This development has attracted growing interest from researchers studying information flows, behavioral economics, and digital communication systems.

Understanding how prediction markets function within modern digital environments requires examining both their technical mechanisms and their social dynamics. These systems are not merely economic tools; they also represent complex arenas in which information, incentives, and human behavior interact.

2. The Mechanism of Information Aggregation

At the heart of prediction markets lies a mechanism for aggregating dispersed information. Participants in the market may possess different types of knowledge—personal expertise, statistical data, or interpretations of recent events. Through buying and selling contracts tied to future outcomes, they express their expectations in a measurable form.

Market prices emerge from this interaction. If many participants believe a particular outcome is likely, demand for contracts associated with that outcome increases, pushing prices upward. Conversely, if confidence declines, prices fall. The resulting price movements can be interpreted as probabilistic estimates of future events.

From an information science perspective, prediction markets function as decentralized systems of knowledge production. Instead of relying on centralized analysis, they distribute the forecasting process across a large population of participants. Each transaction contributes a small piece of information to the collective dataset.

This process is often described as an example of “collective intelligence.” By combining diverse viewpoints, prediction markets may capture insights that would remain hidden in isolated analyses. However, the effectiveness of this mechanism depends heavily on the structure of the market and the behavior of its participants.

3. Data Generation and Analytical Opportunities

Prediction markets generate highly structured data that can be analyzed to study patterns of collective decision-making. Every trade records a participant’s belief about the probability of a particular event, as well as the timing of that belief. Over time, these transactions form a detailed timeline of how expectations evolve.

Researchers have begun to use prediction market data to investigate several key questions. For example, how quickly do participants respond to new information? Do certain types of users consistently anticipate market movements earlier than others? And how do external events—such as news reports or political developments—affect market expectations?

These datasets also allow researchers to observe the dynamics of uncertainty. In periods of stable information environments, prediction prices often fluctuate within narrow ranges. During moments of disruption or breaking news, however, market volatility increases as participants rapidly revise their expectations.

The availability of such data has made prediction markets a valuable laboratory for studying digital behavior at scale. Unlike surveys or controlled experiments, prediction markets capture real decisions made under conditions of risk and uncertainty.

4. Behavioral Dynamics in Prediction Markets

Although prediction markets rely on economic principles, participant behavior is strongly influenced by psychological factors. Traders do not always act as perfectly rational agents. Instead, their decisions may reflect cognitive biases, emotional reactions, or social influences.

One commonly observed phenomenon is herd behavior. When a market price begins to move rapidly in one direction, participants may follow the trend rather than independently evaluating the available information. This behavior can amplify market movements and sometimes lead to temporary distortions in predicted probabilities.

Another important factor is overconfidence. Participants who strongly believe in their own predictions may invest heavily in a particular outcome even when available evidence is ambiguous. While such behavior can sometimes improve market accuracy—especially when informed participants act decisively—it can also increase volatility.

Understanding these behavioral dynamics is essential for evaluating the reliability of prediction markets. Market outcomes do not simply reflect information; they also reflect the ways in which individuals interpret and act upon that information.

5. Prediction Markets in Digital Platforms

The integration of prediction mechanisms into digital platforms has significantly expanded the scope of these systems. Traditional prediction markets were often limited to specialized financial environments, but digital platforms have introduced new forms of participation.

For instance, some online communities use prediction-style systems to forecast outcomes in entertainment contexts, including e-sports competitions or live-streamed events. In these environments, prediction systems often operate with virtual currencies or platform-based reward mechanisms rather than traditional financial contracts.

This shift has important implications for user behavior. When prediction markets are embedded within social platforms, participation may be influenced by community interactions, streaming audiences, or platform-specific incentives. The boundary between forecasting and entertainment becomes increasingly blurred.

For researchers, these environments offer new opportunities to study how prediction systems function when integrated into broader digital ecosystems.

6. Security and Manipulation Risks

As prediction markets grow in scale and visibility, concerns about security and manipulation have become more prominent. Because market prices are often interpreted as indicators of collective belief, attempts to manipulate those prices can have broader informational consequences.

Manipulation may occur when participants attempt to artificially inflate or suppress prices by executing large trades. In some cases, such actions may be intended to create misleading signals about the likelihood of specific events.

Digital platforms must therefore consider mechanisms to protect the integrity of prediction markets. These mechanisms may include transaction monitoring, limits on market participation, or algorithmic systems designed to detect unusual trading patterns.

From a research perspective, studying manipulation attempts can also provide insight into the resilience of digital information systems.

7. Ethical and Regulatory Considerations

Prediction markets operate at the intersection of finance, information exchange, and digital governance. As these systems expand, regulatory frameworks must address several important questions.

One issue concerns the classification of prediction contracts. In some jurisdictions, they may be treated as financial instruments, while in others they may fall under gambling regulations. The regulatory classification can significantly influence how prediction markets are designed and operated.

Another ethical consideration involves accessibility and user protection. When prediction systems are integrated into entertainment platforms or social media environments, younger or less experienced users may participate without fully understanding the associated risks.

Designing prediction systems that balance openness with responsible governance is therefore a key challenge for both platform developers and policymakers.

8. Conclusion: Prediction Markets as Digital Knowledge Systems

Prediction markets represent more than forecasting tools. They function as complex digital environments in which information, incentives, and human behavior intersect. By transforming individual expectations into measurable market signals, these systems provide a unique window into collective decision-making processes.

For researchers in information science, prediction markets offer valuable opportunities to study how distributed knowledge emerges within networked societies. The data generated by these markets reveals how individuals respond to uncertainty, how information spreads through digital communities, and how collective beliefs evolve over time.

As digital platforms continue to evolve, prediction markets are likely to play an increasingly important role in shaping how societies interpret and anticipate future events. Understanding their mechanisms, risks, and potential benefits will therefore remain an important area of interdisciplinary research.
